source_text: ἐπιεικεστέροις ἀσφαλές. Γέγραπται γὰρ «Ὁ συμπορευόμενος σοφοῖς, σοφὸς ἔσται· ὁ δὲ συμπορευόμενος ἄφροσι, γνωσθήσεται.» Γράφει δὲ καὶ ὁ Παῦλος· «Ἐάν τις ἀδελφὸς ὀνομαζόμενος πλεονέκτης, ἢ εἰδωλολάτρης, ἢ λοίδορος, ἢ μέθυσος, ἢ ἅρπαξ, τῷ τοιούτῳ μηδὲ συνεσθίειν.» {ΠΑΛΛ.} Εὖ ἔφης· τὸ γάρ τοι χρῆμά ἐστιν οὐκ ἀσυντελὲς εἰς ὄνησιν. {ΚΥΡ.} Νηκτῶν μὲν δὴ πέρι καὶ τῶν ἐν τοῖς ὕδασι ταυτὶ πρὸς ἡμᾶς αἰνιγματωδῶς ὁ νόμος. Κατευρύνων δὲ ὥσπερ τῶν παραδειγμάτων ἡμῖν τὴν παράθεσιν, ἐπὶ τὰς πτηνῶν ἀγέλας ἐπιφέρει λέγων· «Καὶ ταῦτα
pass_a_gloss: §23 dual gloss: βδελύσσομαι / abominate · πετεινόν / bird · ἑρπετόν / creeping … Pass A ≠ Pass B. Theme: Keep clean company; unclean birds as manner-images.
pass_b_english: Cyril: ...more safely with the more fair ones. For it has been written: 'The one going-with wise ones will be wise; and the one going-with foolish ones will be known.' (Proverbs 13:20) And Paul also writes: 'If someone being named a brother is greedy, or an idolater, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or a plunderer, with such a one not even to eat-with.' (1 Corinthians 5:11)
Palladius: You spoke well; for at least the matter is not unbeneficial unto help.

Cyril: So then about swimming ones and the in the waters these things the law toward us riddlingly. And as it were widening for us the setting-beside of the examples, he brings-on upon the herds of winged ones saying: 'And these you will abominate from the birds, and it will not be eaten; an abomination it is; the eagle and the griffin, and the sea-eagle, and the vulture, and the kite, and the like to it, and sparrow, and owl, and gull, and the like to it, and every raven and the like to it, and hawk and the like to it, and night-raven, and diver, and ibis, and purple-gallinule, and pelican, and swan, and heron, and plover and the like to it, and hoopoe, and bat, and all the creeping of the winged ones which walk upon four, abominations they are for you. But these you will eat from the creeping of the winged ones which walk upon four, which have legs higher than their feet to leap in them upon the earth: the locust and the like, the bald-locust and the like, the serpent-fighter and the like, and the grasshopper and the like. Every creeping from the winged ones for which there are four feet, abominations they are for you, and in these you will be defiled. Everyone touching their carcasses will be unclean until evening.' (Leviticus 11:13–24) So then is the mind of the having-been-said clear for you?
Cyril: Or do you not perceive thereafter that in equal to the others, images of customs and differences of manners would be the natural own things of each of the having-been-named?
Cyril: Do you wish we speak part by part, having distinguished each finely?
